attempts.raw_response: Yet, as the match progressed, a strange calm began to settle over me. The roar of the thousands faded into a distant hum, like the ocean heard from miles away. I stopped thinking about the score or the stakes and simply let my body move with the rhythm of the ball. Each swing became an extension of my will, precise and effortless. He was right; sticking to it mattered more than any outcome. When the final point landed, the noise rushed back in, overwhelming and bright. I looked at him, breathless but smiling. We hadn’t won the way we planned, but we had found something else entirely in that chaos. It wasn’t just about the game anymore. It was about holding onto your center when everything around you tries to pull you apart. That quiet strength remained long after the crowd had gone home.

pair.human_continuation:
I can quite well
remember a dispute going on in the open stand for quite a long time
during the first set. I think a lady would not put down her sunshade;
there was quite a commotion about it. And then people near would shout
advice to me, or scream out, "It's over! Run!" This happened two or
three times; and although I knew they were trying to help me, which in
itself was cheering and encouraging, it was very distracting and
disconcerting. But after some time I lost it all, and became engrossed
in the game. I think in 1907 Miss Sutton was much steadier and played a
better all-round game, but I do not think she had quite the same
terrific fore-hand drive as in the first two years she was over here.
pair.prefix:
Not that I expected him to speak, but
I felt I simply must say something to some one. He told me afterwards he
wanted to say, "I don't know; but stick to it whatever happens!"
Concentration on the game in this match was terribly difficult, as the
crowd was so huge and seemed so excited; it was almost impossible to
forget the people and lose yourself in the game.

source_document.title: Lawn Tennis for Ladies by Mrs. Lambert Chambers
